notes.front: What is a forecast, in Scrum.org's forecasting material?
notes.back: An estimate of future events, trends or outcomes, based on what is known and on analysis of past and present conditions.
notes.explanation: It looks forward, but it is built from information already in hand.
notes.example: Like a weather forecast for the weekend: drawn from today's readings and past patterns, and useful for planning, but not a promise of sunshine.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a product release, in Scrum.org's material?
notes.back: A team delivering a new or updated experience to its customers, to deliver value and gain feedback.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org names both aims: getting value to customers and learning from their response.
notes.example: Like a café putting a new sandwich on the counter this week: people can buy it now, and the staff hear straight away whether they like it.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What can a Scrum Team use release planning for, in Scrum.org's material?
notes.back: To plan delivery as many small, frequent releases rather than one large launch.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org frames release planning around many small deliveries, not one large launch.
notes.example: Like a publisher bringing out a novel chapter by chapter in a magazine instead of waiting to print the whole book at once.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In product development, what does Scrum.org say forecasting is commonly used for in release planning?
notes.back: To align everyone involved and manage their expectations about when new products or features will be delivered.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org places forecasting inside release planning, for everyone involved in the delivery.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On what basis does Scrum.org say a Scrum Team can forecast when Product Backlog items will be delivered?
notes.back: On the team's own trends and history.
notes.explanation: The forecast draws on how the team has actually performed so far.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is a Scrum Team's forecast a commitment or a guarantee, according to Scrum.org?
notes.back: No. It is neither a commitment nor a guarantee.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org gives the reason as the complex nature of the team's work.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From the team's history, a Product Owner forecasts that a feature will probably be ready in about three Sprints. The finance director writes it into a contract as a fixed date. What fits Scrum.org's view?
notes.back: Explain that the forecast is an estimate from past data, not a commitment or guarantee, because the work is complex.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers are now committed to the date
B) Explain that the forecast is an estimate from past data, not a commitment or guarantee, because the work is complex
C) Stop forecasting so nobody can misuse the numbers
notes.choicesExplained: A: Scrum.org says a forecast is by no means a commitment. C: Scrum.org presents forecasting as useful for aligning people and managing expectations.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org separates a forecast from a promise and ties that to the complexity of the work.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two practices the Scrum Guide mentions for forecasting progress?
notes.back: Any two of burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows (the Guide's list is open: “like”).
notes.explanation: The Guide calls these practices proven useful, while saying they do not replace the importance of empiricism.
notes.evidence: Various practices exist to forecast progress, like burn-downs, burn-ups, or cumulative flows. While proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: Do burn-downs and similar forecasting practices replace empiricism, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: No. They are proven useful but do not replace the importance of empiricism.
notes.explanation: The Guide follows this by saying that in complex environments what will happen is unknown.
notes.evidence: While proven useful, these do not replace the importance of empiricism. In complex environments, what will happen is unknown.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: In complex environments, what will happen is unknown, so only {{c1::what has already happened}} may be used for forward-looking decision making.
notes.back: what has already happened
notes.explanation: This is the Guide's statement of empiricism applied to forecasting: decisions rest on what has been observed.
notes.evidence: In complex environments, what will happen is unknown. Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: A team has finished about 12 items a Sprint for six Sprints. A manager asks the Product Owner to draw the release burn-up using 20 a Sprint, “because the team will speed up”. What does the Scrum Guide support?
notes.back: Base the forecast on the team's actual past results, not on hoped-for future speed.
notes.choices:
A) Use 20 a Sprint: forecasts should motivate the team
B) Base the forecast on the team's actual past results, not on hoped-for future speed
C) Drop the burn-up and give no forecast at all
notes.choicesExplained: A: a hoped-for rate has not happened yet, and the Guide allows only what has happened for forward-looking decisions. C: the Guide calls such practices proven useful; the fault is the input, not the chart.
notes.explanation: The Guide says only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decisions.
notes.evidence: Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: Which benefit of frequent small releases, in Scrum.org's list, is about hearing from users sooner?
notes.back: Users can respond sooner, so the team learns and changes course sooner.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org groups feedback, learning and course correction together as one benefit.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of frequent small releases, in Scrum.org's list, comes from catching potential issues earlier?
notes.back: Reduced risk.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org links the lower risk directly to problems surfacing sooner.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which benefit of frequent small releases, in Scrum.org's list, concerns seeing progress toward goals?
notes.back: Better focus and transparency on progress toward goals.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org pairs focus with transparency in this benefit, both aimed at progress toward goals.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides faster feedback, reduced risk, and better focus and transparency, Scrum.org lists {{c1::increased effectiveness}} as a benefit of frequent small releases.
notes.back: increased effectiveness
notes.explanation: It completes Scrum.org's four-item list of benefits.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Product Owner plans to hold back a new booking service for 14 months and launch everything in one go, so it “makes a splash”. Which approach does Scrum.org's release planning guidance favour?
notes.back: Small, incremental, frequent releases, which bring faster feedback and catch issues earlier.
notes.choices:
A) One big launch, so users see the full product at once
B) Small, incremental, frequent releases, which bring faster feedback and catch issues earlier
C) No releases until every Product Backlog item is done
notes.choicesExplained: A: Scrum.org contrasts its approach with big-bang launches. C: waiting for the whole Product Backlog is the big-bang pattern in another form.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org presents release planning as a guide to frequent small releases and lists their benefits.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With continuous integration, delivery and deployment, how often does Scrum.org say a Scrum Team can release?
notes.back: At any point: several times in a Sprint, or even several times a day.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org adds that release planning then covers shorter-term plans, and the team must check that its Increments really deliver value.
notes.source: Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”, “Release Planning”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: May an Increment be delivered to stakeholders before the Sprint ends?
notes.back: Yes. The Scrum Guide says an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before the end of the Sprint.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that the Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
notes.evidence: However, an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: The Sprint Review should never be considered {{c1::a gate to releasing value}}.
notes.back: a gate to releasing value
notes.explanation: Releasing can happen during the Sprint; the Review is where the sum of the Increments is presented.
notes.evidence: The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review thus supporting empiricism. However, an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: How many Increments may a Scrum Team create within one Sprint, and what is presented at the Sprint Review?
notes.back: Multiple Increments may be created; their sum is presented at the Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: The Guide says presenting the sum of the Increments supports empiricism.
notes.evidence: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review thus supporting empiricism.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: On day 3 of a four-week Sprint, a fix that customers badly need meets the Definition of Done. The Product Owner wants to hold it until the Sprint Review so it can be approved there. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: It may be released now: an Increment may be delivered before the Sprint ends, and the Sprint Review is not a release gate.
notes.choices:
A) Hold it: only the Sprint Review can approve a release
B) It may be released now: an Increment may be delivered before the Sprint ends, and the Sprint Review is not a release gate
C) Release it only at the start of the next Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says the Sprint Review should never be a gate to releasing value. C: the Guide allows delivery before the end of the current Sprint, so there is no need to wait.
notes.explanation: Done work forms an Increment, and multiple Increments may be created and delivered within a Sprint.
notes.evidence: Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. The sum of the Increments is presented at the Sprint Review thus supporting empiricism. However, an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint. The Sprint Review should never be considered a gate to releasing value.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: In order to provide value, the Increment must be {{c1::usable}}.
notes.back: usable
notes.explanation: The Guide also says each Increment adds to all prior ones and is thoroughly verified so that they all work together.
notes.evidence: Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: A team's only output this Sprint is a set of screen mock-ups that nobody can use yet. The Developers call it “this Sprint's Increment”. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: It is not an Increment in the Guide's sense: to provide value an Increment must be usable.
notes.choices:
A) It counts, as long as stakeholders like the designs
B) It is not an Increment in the Guide's sense: to provide value an Increment must be usable
C) It counts, because anything produced in a Sprint is an Increment
notes.choicesExplained: A: stakeholders liking the designs does not make them usable. C: the Guide requires an Increment to be usable, and mock-ups nobody can use are not.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties an Increment's value to its being usable.
notes.evidence: In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Increment”

notes.front: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, what may not happen to it?
notes.back: It cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: The bar covers showing the item at the Sprint Review, not only releasing it.
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: Where does a Product Backlog item go if it does not meet the Definition of Done by the end of the Sprint?
notes.back: Back to the Product Backlog, for future consideration.
notes.explanation: It is neither released nor presented; it waits in the Product Backlog to be considered again.
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review. Instead, it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: An item is coded but its required security testing, part of the Definition of Done, is unfinished. A stakeholder asks to have it switched on for customers today “as a beta”. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: It cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review, until it meets the Definition of Done.
notes.choices:
A) Release it as a beta, since it is almost Done
B) It cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review, until it meets the Definition of Done
C) Release it if the Product Owner accepts the risk
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide makes no exception for “almost” Done. C: the Guide gives the Product Owner no power to release work that fails the Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Guide bars undone items from release and from the Sprint Review alike.
notes.evidence: If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: If the Definition of Done is part of the organization's standards, how must Scrum Teams treat it? And if it is not?
notes.back: All Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If there is no such standard, the Scrum Team must create one suited to the product.
notes.explanation: Either way a Definition of Done exists: set by the organization as a floor, or made by the team for its product.
notes.evidence: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: The organization's Definition of Done requires an accessibility check. To release sooner, a Scrum Team proposes dropping that check from its own Definition of Done. What does the Scrum Guide allow?
notes.back: Not dropping it: all Scrum Teams must follow the organizational Definition of Done as a minimum.
notes.choices:
A) Dropping it, since the team is self-managing
B) Dropping it, if the Product Owner agrees
C) Not dropping it: all Scrum Teams must follow the organizational Definition of Done as a minimum
notes.choicesExplained: A: self-management does not override the rule that all Scrum Teams follow the organizational standard as a minimum. B: the Guide gives the Product Owner no power to lower that minimum.
notes.explanation: The Guide leaves the Definition of Done to the team only where there is no organizational standard; here there is one.
notes.evidence: If the Definition of Done for an increment is part of the standards of the organization, all Scrum Teams must follow it as a minimum. If it is not an organizational standard, the Scrum Team must create a Definition of Done appropriate for the product.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Definition of Done”

notes.front: Sprints are fixed length events of {{c1::one month or less}} to create consistency.
notes.back: one month or less
notes.explanation: The Guide says Sprints enable predictability by making sure progress toward the Product Goal is inspected and adapted at least every calendar month.
notes.evidence: They are fixed length events of one month or less to create consistency.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: To match a quarterly release plan, a Product Owner proposes six-week Sprints. What does the Scrum Guide say?
notes.back: Not allowed: Sprints are fixed length events of one month or less.
notes.choices:
A) Fine, if the whole Scrum Team agrees
B) Not allowed: Sprints are fixed length events of one month or less
C) Fine, as long as each Sprint still has a Sprint Review
notes.choicesExplained: A: team agreement does not change the one-month limit. C: holding the events does not make a six-week Sprint allowed.
notes.explanation: The one-month limit is part of the Guide's definition of the Sprint, whatever the release plan says.
notes.evidence: They are fixed length events of one month or less to create consistency.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: What does the Scrum Guide say shorter Sprints can be used for?
notes.back: To generate more learning cycles and limit the risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that each Sprint may be considered a short project.
notes.evidence: Shorter Sprints can be employed to generate more learning cycles and limit risk of cost and effort to a smaller time frame. Each Sprint may be considered a short project.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “The Sprint”

notes.front: At Sprint Planning, knowing which three things makes the Developers more confident in their Sprint forecasts?
notes.back: Their past performance, their upcoming capacity and their Definition of Done.
notes.explanation: The Guide admits that selecting how much can be completed within a Sprint may be challenging.
notes.evidence: Selecting how much can be completed within a Sprint may be challenging. However, the more the Developers know about their past performance, their upcoming capacity, and their Definition of Done, the more confident they will be in their Sprint forecasts.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Planning”, Topic Two

notes.front: How does a release forecast differ from the Sprint Goal in what it binds the team to?
notes.back: A forecast is neither a commitment nor a guarantee; the Sprint Goal is a commitment by the Developers.
notes.explanation: Scrum.org calls forecasts non-binding estimates, while the Scrum Guide names the Sprint Goal as the Developers' commitment for the Sprint.
notes.evidence: The Sprint Goal is the single objective for the Sprint. Although the Sprint Goal is a commitment by the Developers, it provides flexibility in terms of the exact work needed to achieve it.
notes.source: The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Commitment: Sprint Goal”; Scrum.org learning series, “Forecasting and Release Planning”
